In an estuarine ecosystem, biotic (living) and abiotic (non-living) factors are deeply interconnected. Abiotic factors such as salinity, temperature, tides, and nutrient levels dictate which species can survive. In turn, biotic factors like plants, algae, and animals influence these conditions through processes such as filtration, oxygen production, and sediment stabilization. This dynamic equilibrium is maintained through intricate feedback loops; for example, mangroves or salt marsh grasses stabilize soil (abiotic) while providing habitat (biotic), which in turn supports biodiversity that helps regulate water quality and nutrient cycling, ensuring the ecosystem remains balanced despite constant environmental fluctuations.
